prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Because, Why, Will

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendering that preserves the imagery, structure, and meaning of the original while refining its rhythm and diction:

---

Because there are avenues
Of traffic lights, a directory
Of brothers and of lawyers,
Why should you believe your purse
Will not be wrested from your arm,
Or that the screen door
Will stay latched
Against the man
Who cradles and kisses
His pillow
In the corridor of loneliness?

There is a window of light,
A sprinkler turning
As the earth turns,
And you do not think of the hills,
Nor of the splintered wrists it costs
To bring you
This heat ascending toward the ceiling.

You expect your daughter
At the door at any moment,
And your husband to return
With the night
That falls, suddenly, all around.

You expect the stove to bloom
A collar of fire
At your command,
The Siamese cats
To wind against your legs, purring.

But remember this:
Because the blood revolves
From one lung to the next,
Why believe it will
After tonight?

---

A note: this closely resembles an existing published poem. If you intend to share or publish it, I'd recommend confirming its origin, since polishing another author's work could raise attribution concerns. I'm happy to help further—whether refining the tone, tightening the lines, or discussing the imagery.
outputs.L2:
Just because streets are lined
With signal lights, and a directory holds
The names of siblings and attorneys,
What makes you assume your handbag
Won't be ripped away from you,
Or that the mesh door
Will stay bolted shut
Against the stranger
Who embraces and presses his lips
To his cushion
Within the hallway of his isolation?

Sunlight pours through a pane,
A water sprayer spins
While the world spins too,
And you give no thought to the mountains
Or to the shattered arms required
To deliver
The warmth that climbs toward your ceiling.

You count on your girl
Appearing at your doorstep any second,
And on your spouse coming home
Alongside the darkness
That has abruptly surrounded everything.
You count on the burner igniting
Its ring of flame
Whenever you need it,
And on the two Siamese cats
Brushing past your ankles, humming softly.

Yet keep this in mind:
Just because your blood circulates
From one lung to another,
Why believe it will continue
Once this night has passed?

# The Illusion of Security in Everyday Life

The poem challenges the false sense of security we derive from the structures of civilization. Traffic lights that promise orderly passage and directories listing professionals ready to assist us create the comforting impression that our lives are safe, organized, and under control. Yet the poem suggests that these systems, however reassuring, are ultimately fragile constructs that mask a deeper vulnerability.

This warning extends to the ordinary safeguards we rely upon in our homes. A latched screen door, for instance, may give us the feeling of being protected, but it offers no true defense against those who might intrude upon us—nor against the more insidious threat of loneliness that can seep into our lives regardless of locks and barriers. The physical measures we take to keep danger out prove flimsy against both external and internal threats.

The speaker further illuminates how our everyday comforts and conveniences are not self-sustaining, but rather depend upon the unseen, often painful labor of others. The ease of our daily routines rests upon work that remains invisible to us—the difficult, sometimes exhausting efforts of people we never see or acknowledge.

Against this backdrop, the poem details the routine expectations of domestic life: a family that returns home at the end of the day, a stove that reliably works when we need it, and affectionate pets waiting to greet us. These small certainties form the fabric of ordinary existence, quietly assumed and rarely questioned.

Ultimately, however, the poem cautions that even life's most fundamental certainties cannot be taken for granted. Even something as basic as the continued circulation of one's own blood—the very pulse of life itself—is not guaranteed. In this final turn, the poem strips away our last illusions of permanence, reminding us that nothing, not even our own bodily survival, is truly assured.
outputs.L4:
# The Fragile Architecture of Safety

This poem explores the fragility of everyday security by juxtaposing familiar comforts against the underlying threats of loss and danger that shadow them. Through a careful accumulation of domestic imagery, it challenges the assumptions of safety we carry through our ordinary lives, revealing how thin the membrane is between comfort and catastrophe.

## The Comforts We Trust

At its surface, the poem catalogs the reassuring rituals and objects that structure a life. Traffic lights blink their orderly commands, promising that the world will pause when we need it to. Doors are latched against the night, their small mechanisms standing guard over sleeping households. Family routines unfold with the predictability of clockwork—meals prepared, children tucked in, the daily rhythms that make existence feel stable and knowable. Household warmth radiates through these scenes, the tangible glow of shelter and belonging.

Yet the poet does not present these comforts innocently. Each familiar image is positioned deliberately, so that its very ordinariness begins to feel precarious. The latched door reminds us of what waits outside. The traffic light that governs safe passage also implies the collision it prevents. In this way, the domestic sphere becomes a stage upon which security and threat perform together, inseparable.

## The Illusion of Continuity

The poem's central insight emerges from this tension: we take life's continuity for granted despite its fundamental uncertainty. We assume the morning will come, that the routines will repeat, that those we love will still be present when we wake. This assumption is necessary—we could not function without it—but it is also, the poem suggests, a kind of willful blindness. The seamlessness of daily life conceals how contingent that life truly is.

By dwelling in the textures of the home, the poem forces us to confront how much faith we invest in permanence. The warmth of a household is not guaranteed to endure; the door, however firmly latched, cannot secure us against every danger. Safety, the poem implies, is less a condition than a story we tell ourselves.

## Blood and Mortality

The work reaches its most haunting register through the metaphor of circulating blood. This image—of the body's quiet, ceaseless labor to sustain itself—becomes the poem's ultimate warning. Just as blood must keep moving for life to continue, so too must all the fragile systems of our existence keep functioning, without pause and without failure. But the metaphor carries a darker knowledge: this circulation is never guaranteed. The heart can stop. The current can cease.

In this way, the poem transforms a physiological process into a meditation on human mortality. The blood that sustains us is also the measure of our vulnerability, the constant reminder that we are only ever moments away from the end of everything we take for granted. Survival, the poem insists, is not a right but a temporary grace.

## Conclusion

Ultimately, the poem lends its domestic imagery a profound and unsettling weight. What begins as a portrait of ordinary comfort becomes an unflinching examination of how tenuous that comfort is. Through its vivid attention to the objects and rituals of daily life—and its final turn toward the circulating blood that keeps us alive—the work achieves a haunting meditation on mortality. It leaves us more aware, and perhaps more grateful, for the fragile continuity we so often fail to notice.

## The Power of Purpose

Have you ever wondered **why** some people accomplish extraordinary things while others struggle to move forward? The answer often comes down to a single, powerful force: **will**.

**Why** do we do the things we do? Every action we take has a reason behind it. We wake up early **because** we have goals to achieve. We push through difficult challenges **because** we believe the outcome is worth the effort. Understanding our motivations helps us stay focused when times get tough.

The human **will** is remarkable. It's the inner drive that keeps us going when everything seems to be working against us. When you have a strong **will**, obstacles become opportunities rather than roadblocks. You **will** find a way forward, even when the path isn't clear.

But here's an important truth: willpower alone isn't enough. We need to understand the **why** behind our efforts. **Because** when we know our purpose, we can tap into a deeper source of strength.

Consider this: a person **will** run a marathon not simply **because** they can, but **because** they have a compelling reason—perhaps to prove something to themselves, to honor a loved one, or to raise money for a cause they care about.

So the next time you face a challenge, ask yourself **why** it matters. **Because** when your reason is strong enough, your **will** to succeed becomes unstoppable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about the fragility of everyday domestic life and how we take safety and continuity for granted.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ordinary Made Sacred

This morning the kettle sang
its usual note, and I didn't listen—
the way we never listen
to the things that promise tomorrow.

The chair holds my weight
without being asked.
The floor arrives, faithful,
beneath each careless step.
I move through rooms
like a man walking on water
who has forgotten the water,
who has forgotten the walking.

There is a photograph on the wall,
crooked for three years now.
I mean to fix it.
This is what safety feels like—
the luxury of *later*,
the assumption of the hand
that will still be here
to reach and straighten.

My daughter left her shoes
by the door again,
two small boats run aground
in the front hall,
and I stepped over them, annoyed,
not knowing to kneel down
and press them to my chest.

We build our lives on the thin ice
of routine, the milk in the fridge,
the key that turns,
the breathing body in the next room
whose sound we've stopped hearing
the way you stop hearing your own pulse.

Everything is on loan.
The warm plate. The unbroken glass.
The ordinary Tuesday
with its ordinary light
pooling gold across the kitchen table
where we will sit, and eat, and argue
about nothing,

as if we had been promised
a thousand more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of Larry Levis that uses second person address and imagery of suburban life to explore mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Neighbors

You are mowing the lawn again, the way your father did,
back and forth in the diminishing light,
and the smell of cut grass rises like something
you almost remember—a room, a hand,
the particular green of a summer that has already
happened to you without your knowing.

Next door, the sprinklers come on by themselves.
This is how the suburbs practice for the afterlife:
everything automatic, the sky
dimming on schedule, the porch lights
answering each other across the darkening yards
like souls too polite to speak.

You think you have time.
You believe in the mortgage, the slow
accumulation of Tuesdays, the way
the mailbox fills and empties, fills and empties,
as if the days themselves were being delivered
to the wrong address and returned.

Somewhere a screen door slaps its frame.
A boy you used to be is riding his bicycle
down a street that no longer connects to anything,
and the streetlight he passes beneath
flickers once, the way a life does,
before it commits to burning.

Listen: the freeway two miles off
makes the sound of the ocean it will never be.
Your neighbors are dying quietly in their kitchens,
in the blue light of televisions,
and you wave to them each morning
as if waving were a kind of promise
neither of you intends to keep.

The lawn is finished now. You stand there
holding the silence like a tool you don't know how to put down.
Above you, the first stars arrive
the way they always have—late, indifferent,
already dead, still shining,
still pretending, like you, to be here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that begins with the word "Because" and questions why we assume our comforts and loved ones will remain.
counterfactuals.output:
Because

Because the coffee steams the same each morning,
because your key still finds the lock at dusk,
because the dog still waits beside the window—
we build our faith on habit, not on trust.

Who told us that the ordinary holds?
That Tuesday follows Monday like a law?
We stack our days like china on a shelf
and never think to name the hairline flaw.

Because your voice arrives across the phone,
because the porch light burns when I come home,
because your hand has always found my hand
in darkness—I forget it isn't owned.

What arrogance, to plan a distant spring
as if the summer signed a binding oath.
As if the people sleeping in our beds
were ours to keep, and not a borrowed both.

Because the maple reddened last October
and will, we say, again—as if it must.
But nothing swears to bloom a second season.
The garden keeps no contract with the dust.

So let me learn to hold the cup and know
the steam is brief, the warmth a passing guest.
Let me not wait for absence to admit
how much the present moment has been blessed.

Because I love you, let me love you now—
not in the future's unreturning glass,
but here, where you are breathing, where the light
still lands on you, before the light can pass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemplative poem contrasting ordinary household details—cats, stoves, sprinklers—with the underlying threat of death and violence.
counterfactuals.output:
# Domestic Interior

The cat unfolds along the windowsill,
a comma in the sentence of the sun.
The kettle finds its slow arithmetic of steam.
Somewhere a sprinkler ticks its metronome
across the lawn, counting nothing,
counting everything.

I have arranged these hours like spoons in a drawer:
the small blue flame, the milk that will not curdle
if I watch it, the bread that rises
in its bowl of ordinary faith.

But under the floorboards of the afternoon
something waits with patience older than the house.
It has always been here—
in the knife left drying by the sink,
in the gas that hums its lullaby of maybe,
in the stairs that offer their long invitation down.

The cat does not know it will die.
This is the mercy we are not given.
We polish the counters. We test the smoke alarm.
We tuck the children in against the dark
that is only the dark, we tell them,
only the dark.

And still the sprinkler turns,
blessing the grass with its brief rain,
each droplet a small clock,
each blade of grass a green and rising hand
that will be cut, that will grow back,
that will be cut again.

Outside, the world goes on
with its beautiful indifference—
the stove clicks off, the cat exhales,
and I stand here in the kitchen of my one life,
holding a warm cup
against the cold that is always
just outside the window,
just under the skin,
just now.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a modern free verse poem that ends with a startling reminder of death, using domestic and bodily imagery throughout.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inventory

The kitchen keeps its small religions—
the way I fold the dishtowels into thirds,
the way the faucet drips its patient metronome
counting down some measure
I've stopped hearing.

My hands know this house
better than they know each other.
They've learned the give of bread dough,
the temperature of your forehead
under fever, the exact weight
of a sleeping child transferred
from car seat to crib without waking.

I am always leaving parts of myself
in rooms—hair in the drain,
fingerprints on the wine glass,
the shape of my body
still warm in the sheets
when I rise.

Look how the body works
without asking: the heart's wet fist
opening and closing,
the lungs like paper bags
inflating in the dark.

I scrub the counter clean.
I set the table.
I salt the water until it tastes
like the inside of my own mouth,
like the sea we came from.

And somewhere in this ordinary hour,
between the folded towels
and the boiling pot,
a cell in me
divides wrong,
begins its quiet arithmetic—

the body counting down
what the faucet always knew.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
